## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There are no results yet. The starting architecture scored 0.000 on both seeds, so any gain will be easy to see but hard to attribute. The default recipe runs only 32 PPO updates of 4,096 samples each, with 4 epochs on every sample. With a stream of fresh designs and a dense reward, more samples and more updates are probably worth more than extra epochs. A net cost r below 1 earns no extra samples, so architectures should stay near r≈1. On the task side, picking a correct placement depends on the layer the brick lands on: the highest filled cell under its footprint. The starting network never shows the head the target layer by layer. Plan: P1 changes only the recipe (2 epochs, smaller updates). P3 pushes the same idea further (1 epoch). P2 uses the P1 recipe with a per-layer network that pools over each footprint and picks the layer, so P1 against P2 isolates the architecture.

### Round 2
All three trials scored 0 on dev and on training success, including runs with up to 3x more samples. So more data alone does not help, and the per-layer network did no better. My guess about the cause is unconfirmed. Under random play, placements on average add more extra cells than target cells, so each placement's reward is negative, while DONE scores 0. PPO may therefore learn to stop at once before it finds good placements. Neither the network nor sample count would matter then, which fits every result. This round tests two anti-collapse recipes on the baseline network: one with higher entropy and lower lr, and one with even higher entropy and longer horizons that weight the exact-build bonus more. The third trial runs a deeper network with a learned head over each brick's footprint under the first recipe. If any trial scores above 0, it beats the all-zero results so far.

### Round 3
All six trials score exactly 0, on dev and in training (last 10%). That holds across recipes (1 or 2 epochs, entropy 0.005 to 0.05, gamma up to 0.99), a deeper trunk and a per-layer network. Seed noise cannot produce zeros everywhere. On the task as described, a network that learns to fill missing cells should sometimes build a 6-brick design exactly, especially while it still samples actions at random during training. So the cause is probably structural, not a tuning problem. Every network so far assumes that action (t, y, x) lines up with obs cell (y, x) and anchors at the top-left. Translation-equivariant convolutions cannot learn around a flip, a transpose or a permutation of action positions. The task warns that the world may differ from its description, and a layout mismatch is the main thing those networks could not learn around. This round tests that guess directly: two candidates mix several layout hypotheses through a learned gate, and one learns a general remapping of positions.

### Round 4
All 9 trials scored exactly 0, in training as well as on dev. That includes recipe sweeps over epochs, entropy, lr and gamma, a deeper trunk, a per-layer network, a dihedral gate and a dense action remap. If the world matched its description, a 1x1 policy that places bricks on target cells at the landing layer should learn quickly and build some small designs exactly. A hard zero everywhere therefore points to a mismatch between the network's outputs and the env's action layout, not to capacity or recipe. Ruled out so far: flips and transpositions with type-major order and DONE last, and per-type anchor or footprint offsets, which the 3x3 heads covered. Not yet tested: other orderings of the type/y/x axes in the action index (for example type-minor), and DONE sitting at index 0. If DONE sits at index 0, the agent can never stop, so success is impossible. This last round covers these with cheap output-side gates plus a per-action global term, and adds a layout-free attention head as a hedge.
